analysis.one_liner: Creates a regulator whose only job is policing predatory fees, terms, and products in consumer credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Durbin in September 2008 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an independent, five-member Consumer Credit Safety Commission whose sole mission would be protecting people who borrow — much as product safety agencies protect people who buy goods. It could ban predatory or deceptive credit products and features, and its jurisdiction would cover not just interest rates but the full stack of fees consumers actually pay: late fees, over-limit fees, cash advance fees, credit insurance, and even interchange and other payment-system fees. It would also run a consumer complaint hotline, study industry practices, impose civil penalties per transaction, and allow criminal charges of up to $500,000 and one year in prison for executives who knowingly sell banned credit products. The bill's own findings argue that the existing multi-agency structure spread consumer protection responsibility so thin that predatory credit products flourished unchecked.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers — credit card holders, people with mortgages, car loans, and payday loans, and small businesses (which the bill counts as consumers). They would gain a dedicated regulator empowered to ban the abusive fees and product features that push them into unmanageable debt, a hotline to lodge complaints, and penalties that could fund restitution. Honest lenders would also gain a single, predictable rulebook instead of rules scattered across ten agencies.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member independent Commission whose sole job is protecting credit consumers, empowered to ban 'abusive, fraudulent, unfair, deceptive, predatory, anticompetitive, or otherwise anti-consumer' practices and product features.

Brings hidden costs — late fees, over-limit fees, interchange fees, and add-on insurance — under a regulator's explicit jurisdiction, targeting the charges that borrowers often do not see when they take on debt.

Requires the regulator to consider the special needs of elderly people and people with disabilities when writing rules, and to run a public hotline where consumers can file complaints and get help against anti-consumer lending.

Imposes criminal penalties of up to $500,000 and one year in prison on executives who knowingly and willfully offer banned credit products, and civil penalties per transaction for violators, with penalty money available for restitution to harmed consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer credit providers — banks and card issuers, payday and consumer lenders, credit insurers, and payment networks — would bear compliance costs, civil penalties set per transaction, and the loss of profitable fee streams and banned products. Taxpayers would fund the new Commission's operations. Some costs could be passed on to borrowers in the price of credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in federal appropriations, adding a new agency and its staffing to the federal budget without specifying a cost.

A single Commission would make binding rules across nearly all consumer credit, and its stronger rules would supersede those of ten existing agencies where they conflict — concentrating enormous power in five appointed commissioners and risking rules that restrict credit products some consumers genuinely want or need.

Because the Commission can restrict fees and charge billions in penalties against lenders, some of those costs could be passed back to consumers through higher prices or reduced availability of credit, a tradeoff the bill requires the Commission to weigh but does not eliminate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was large: a single regulator charged only with consumer protection, with power to ban specific predatory products, could have addressed problems that a dispersed, bank-supervised regulatory structure demonstrably failed to catch before the 2008 crisis. The costs are real but modest by comparison: the bill creates a new federal bureaucracy funded by taxpayers or penalties, adds a second layer of rulemaking on top of existing bank regulators, and aggressive restrictions could raise the price of credit or push some borrowers toward less-regulated products. Some legitimate lenders would bear compliance costs for the misconduct of others. A version of this idea was ultimately enacted two years later as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which has faced the same objections. The core tradeoff — protecting borrowers from predatory products versus the compliance cost to credit providers — was never debated in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in the middle of the financial crisis, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on September 26, 2008, days after Lehman Brothers' collapse, as Congress was confronting the failure of the financial regulatory structure.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no visible support beyond its author.
The Senate referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer credit providers kept the existing multi-agency regulatory structure, where no regulator has consumer protection as its sole mission, with no new restrictions on fees or products.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but could not attract a single cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a partisan vote; it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so its lack of support crossed party lines.

industries.note: The bill puts their card fees, penalty charges, and credit products under a single regulator empowered to ban any feature it finds predatory, with per-transaction civil penalties and potential criminal liability for executives. They would lose the ability to forum-shop among ten friendly banking regulators.

Products like high-cost short-term loans are squarely 'consumer credit' under the bill and could be restricted or banned outright. These lenders profit from fees that trap borrowers in debt, exactly the conduct the bill targets.

The bill's definition of consumer credit explicitly covers interchange fees, merchant discount fees, and debit card fees, opening those rates to federal safety rules for the first time. Consumers ultimately pay these fees in higher prices.

industries.industry: Credit insurers and add-on product sellers
industries.note: Credit insurance premiums and all ancillary products sold with a loan fall under the Commission's jurisdiction and could be restricted as abusive or deceptive. Consumers who are pressured into these products would gain; the sellers would lose a high-margin revenue stream.

The bill's stated purpose includes giving sellers of consumer credit 'more regulatory certainty', and it lets industry submit voluntary standards that the Commission can adopt directly. Large incumbents with compliance departments could absorb a single set of rules better than small lenders.
